factors.desc: Favorable or neutral coverage across the meta's IP archetypes and color strategies. With an expanded 15-deck meta field, decks with fewer polarized matchups perform more reliably across tournament swiss rounds.
Efficient AP usage and energy curve optimization for early and mid-game board development. Includes the ability to deploy threats ahead of curve and maintain proactive pressure.
Maximum damage output potential through Impact, Double Attack, Damage 2, and high BP thresholds. Measures how decisively a deck can close games once its win condition is assembled.
Overall value and composition of triggers in the deck's life area, including Color triggers for resource generation, Active triggers for board impact, and Final triggers for last-resort defense.
Reliable access to key characters and combo pieces through draw, search, and filtering effects. Decks that consistently assemble their core strategy outperform those reliant on natural draws.
Energy and AP economy, hand size management, and long-term card advantage. Measures how efficiently a deck converts its resources into board presence and damage over the course of a game.
Decision tree depth, AP sequencing complexity, and the gap between average and optimal play lines. Decks that reward mastery with significantly higher win rates score well here.
Ability to recover from life damage pressure, board wipes, and resource deficit through trigger activations, defensive keywords, and comeback mechanics.
Adaptable game plans, multi-color tech options, and the ability to pivot between aggressive and defensive postures depending on game state and matchup.

Ability to interfere with the opponent's board state, hand, or game plan through removal, Snipe, retire effects, and denial of key setups. Increasingly relevant as combo-oriented IPs populate the meta.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Ichigo Raid Midrange asks the pilot to choose among several Ichigo curve options, when to commit the Raid chain, and whether to spend AP on energy-line development or on Bankai and Getsugatensho bursts, which places it above a plain beatdown deck within the Union Arena Standard field. Raid timing, the energy line's colored requirements and holding removal for the right blocker raise sequencing and punishment, though the core Ichigo line is fairly direct once a suitable board exists, so autopilot remains moderate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Heisuke aggro is a fast, straightforward deck: most turns present a clear development line of cheap characters and attacks, so per-turn decisions are moderate rather than dense. Its main skill demands are matchup-aware attacking (knowing when to push into large blockers versus hold back) and resource management for the hand, which can empty by turns 5-6, and a misplayed race is punished against fast opposing tempo decks. The cards do much of the work on a good draw, which keeps the autopilot score high.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Standard Union Arena, this midrange Green deck makes a moderate number of meaningful decisions per turn around energy-line building, Raid timing into Hyorinmaru, and when to commit Bankai, but the core curve of high-BP Kenpachi bodies is fairly direct to pilot. Sequencing matters at key moments such as Raid windows and holding Bankai, while the strongest draws win by playing the obvious plays, which keeps autopilot high. Misplays in the energy line or mulligans against fast Aggro-Tempo decks are costly, so error punishment sits moderately above average.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Rem Raid Aggro asks for a moderate number of decisions per turn: sequencing Subaru plays to fill the energy line, choosing which Subaru to raid onto, and deciding when to attack with a raided Rem, but the core line is fairly clear. Timing matters mainly through Raid sequencing and avoiding stranded Rems, not through instant-speed responses. Errors are meaningful, since a Rem hand without a Subaru stalls and losing a raided character also costs the Subaru, but the strong aggressive curve gives some forgiveness. The deck plays largely on its cards, so a new pilot keeps much of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Bomb Devil raid sequencing, choosing which front-line bodies to raid and how to spend AP against the energy line gives several real decisions per turn, and the matchup plan shifts against large-BP walls and fast defenders. Timing and punishment sit mid-range since the deck has few reactive windows, while its dense 4-of cheap curve and direct raid damage let a straightforward aggressive line win much of the time, lowering the pilot's share of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Union Arena Standard tournament decks, this raid-tempo deck asks for frequent decisions about when to set up the base-plus-raid pair, how to spend AP, and when to attack, and sequencing the raid chain matters. Its plan shifts noticeably between fast aggro matchups and slower control matchups, and a misplayed base or raid setup can cost the game, while the deep 4-copy core keeps it from being overly punishing to pilot.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Midrange Shin Asakura Yellow offers several meaningful choices per turn: when to deploy versus hold, which Raid upgrade to chain onto an already-switched-active character, and how to spend AP and energy. Its early curve and Raid chains are fairly straightforward to execute, so many turns follow an obvious line, while the Raid cards stranded without targets punish sloppy hand management. Sequencing matters mainly in the Raid chain and in choosing the attack timing around a resilient board, and matchup plans shift between aggro and defensive opponents without changing its core identity dramatically.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Raid Midrange asks for real choices each turn about which Byakuya to play, how to spend AP and when to commit, and the Raid text is easy to lose if plays are misordered, so the sequencing and error costs sit above the simplest Standard decks. The deck wins a good deal on its card pool and smooth Raid chains, so a pilot playing the obvious curve keeps much of its win rate, but close games turn on Bankai timing and matchup reads against fast aggro and high-BP walls.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Midrange Evangelion 13 Purple asks for a steady run of decisions each turn: when to commit AP and energy to a heavy unit, which cheap characters to deploy to build the energy line, and when to hold removal such as Longinus. Timing matters moderately, mostly in choosing when to switch AP cards to resting and when to commit the big top-end, rather than in precise response windows. The plan shifts meaningfully against fast aggro (Sakamoto Days, Demon Slayer, One Punch Man) versus slower decks, and misjudging the energy-line race or a stumbled early hand is punished, while the powerful top end means a competent draw still wins a fair share of games on its own.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this Red Kenshin midrange has a moderate number of real decisions per turn, centered on which Kenshin Raid piece to play and when to start Raid chains, which the high skill_ceiling and consistency factors suggest. Its sequencing matters for Raid timing, but the deck is mostly straightforward to execute, so timing sensitivity sits in the middle. Matchup handling (racing aggro versus controlling the board) and the cost of misplaying a Raid chain give it moderate, not extreme, variance and punishment, while a good draw of Kenshin pieces does a fair share of the work on its own.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Green Midrange deck makes several real decisions per turn: when to build the energy line with Shunsui and Nanao, and when to hold back for a Raid swing with Karamatsu Shinju. Its Raid timing and the need to protect the life area against aggro lists add sequencing and matchup demands above the typical tournament deck, but its many dependable openings keep it from being as punishing or as demanding as the most intricate builds.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Mayuri Kurotsuchi midrange asks for a steady stream of energy-line, AP-switching and Raid-target decisions each turn, with Bankai burst timing and matchup-dependent plan shifts (slower decks favorable, Rem and Zenitsu punishing) adding weight. Its 4-copy core makes the early line fairly forgiving, but a misjudged Raid or a late Bankai window can cost the game, so it sits in the middle of the Standard field rather than at the extremes.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Cinderella is a redundant, low-variance midrange deck: sixteen Cinderella copies and cheap yellow bodies make most turns obvious, so decisions are mainly about spending AP efficiently and when to commit to attacks. Sequencing is modest, and its lack of disruption and finisher means matchup knowledge matters somewhat, but the deck wins largely from a consistent draw played the straightforward way.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Chainsaw Man Red Aggro is a fairly straightforward aggro deck: its turns mostly reduce to filling the energy line with cheap Pochita, Denji and Power bodies and then attacking, with a few real choices about event timing and when to commit Chainsaw Man finishers. Its main difficulty lies in managing a drained hand and deciding when to pressure versus hold back against walls and faster aggro, while its cheap curve and high-BP finishers let the cards carry much of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Arima midrange offers a moderate number of meaningful choices per turn, mainly in sequencing energy-line setup against AP usage and deciding when to commit Arima front-liners. Timing sensitivity is modest since there is little response-window play with only one event, while matchup variance is moderate given the notable slow-versus-fast matchup gaps. Mistakes are fairly punishable against aggro decks, but the high-BP Arima bodies and easy energy line let a straightforward pilot win much of the time.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena tournament decks, this Soshiro midrange list makes a moderate number of real choices each turn around energy lines, AP spending and when to commit, but its redundant six-printing Soshiro core and Mina Ashiro energy plan keep most turns fairly obvious. Timing and error punishment are moderate, since the deck has little interaction on the opponent's turn and its tempo deficit against fast decks is mostly structural rather than a sequencing trap; the draw does a lot of the work, so the autopilot score is high.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: A midrange Blue Bleach list with a dense early energy-line curve and a Grimmjow finisher asks for several meaningful Main Phase choices per turn, weighing when to commit characters versus hold AP, plus sideline and removal-area bookkeeping. Its skill ceiling is moderate: the Yoruichi spread makes draws uneven and the obvious lines usually work, but racing against fast Aggro-Tempo decks punishes poor sequencing and late Grimmjow timing, so a competent pilot is needed to convert close games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Beatrice is a midrange-control deck whose skill_ceiling and resource_management factors are moderately high, so turns involve real choices about when to deploy Raid links and how to spend AP and energy, but the cheap, redundant curve keeps most turns fairly obvious. Its main difficulty is matchup-driven: it must recognize when it is behind against fast Aggro-Tempo decks and when to play its slow value game, while errors are moderately punished because the deck has no finisher and a slow start. Its strong, consistent cards mean a competent but unexceptional pilot still wins a reasonable share of games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: A Tier 2 midrange deck with easy mono-green energy and a consistent mid-game board, so most turns have an obvious line with a few real choices in which Kusuri Yakuzen to play at each AP cost. Its main difficulty is matchup-dependent: it loses to fast decks and must read whether to race or stabilize, while the cards do much of the work on a good draw.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, Roy Mustang Blue Midrange is a moderately demanding but straightforward deck: its consistent Roy and Riza core makes the turns mostly obvious, with a few real decisions around energy lines and when to deploy versus hold. Its slow tempo and weak trigger impact mean misplays are costly in races, but its value-oriented grind gives the pilot room to recover, and the cards do much of the work.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Raid sequencing forces many card-by-card choices each turn with a tight 3 AP ceiling, so decisions per turn are high and mistakes in ordering or AP allocation are costly. Awkward Raid hands and slow early turns make the deck hard to keep on track, and winning depends on pilot choices more than raw cards. Its power ceiling is high, but the deck does not play itself, and a new pilot would lose much of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Rimuru midrange asks for regular decisions each Main Phase about which Rimuru to commit, when to use Report and Feast, and how to hit Blue energy on the curve, but the core line is fairly readable. Sequencing and timing matter at a few key moments, mainly around Raid and stacking windows, rather than constantly. The deck's large Rimuru redundancy and its hand-refill cards cushion misplays, though a mismatched draw without Soei can stumble badly. Overall it sits in the middle of the Standard competitive field: more thinking than a straightforward aggro list, yet a good draw played the obvious way still wins many games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Royal Guard midrange deck is fairly straightforward to play: the core plan of building the energy line and Raiding with Senjumaru or Ichibe is clear, so turns have several meaningful choices but few deeply branching lines. Its skill ceiling comes from managing AP and energy-line sequencing in the Main Phase and choosing when to commit Bankai, while misplays are costly mainly in slow openings against faster decks.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Evangelion Raid deck is a mid-tier aggro-tempo list whose core plan is a repeatable Raid line (Production Model-02 into Beast Form) that a new pilot can execute fairly directly, so the autopilot factor is above average. Its decisions center on AP spending, reaching the energy line early, and choosing which base characters and front-line attackers to commit, while weak triggers and a lack of early defense make it more punishing against fast opposing aggro decks.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Red Yuji is a mid-tier aggro-tempo deck whose Raid chains and energy-line sequencing require deliberate turn planning, pushing decision density and sequencing demands above a straightforward beatdown list. Errors are punished because the deck has little draw or search and triggers rarely stabilize, so a misordered Raid or a hand without an energy-line body can lose the race. Its cards do a fair share of the work, but a new pilot would still lose much of its win rate without correct timing and matchup awareness.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Tier 5 Nano Eiai midrange deck runs a predictable early energy line and a consistent mid-curve, so most turns have one obvious play and few sequencing traps. Its skill demand sits below the typical competitive deck because it lacks reach, disruption and strong triggers, meaning the pilot's main job is trading board presence and reading the race against aggro decks like Sakamoto Days and One Punch Man, which keeps matchup and punishment modest rather than extreme.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Rem is a midrange-tempo deck whose core loop is simple: play Ram early, Raid Rem onto it, and attack, with heavy Rem redundancy meaning most draws do the same thing. Decisions arise in choosing when to Raid versus hold, which stacks to build, and how to spend AP, but most turns have an obvious line. Its modest power ceiling and lack of disruption put it in the middle of the Standard field, where stronger midrange and racing decks demand more pilot judgment.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this midrange Red list has a moderate number of real decisions per turn: sequencing cheap characters onto the energy line, deciding when to spend AP on Aki Raid, and choosing between holding Fire!/Easy Revenge! and committing the board. Timing matters at key moments, but the Aki and Himeno copies are near-duplicates and the game plan is fairly stable, so the pilot is rarely forced into deep sequencing traps. The deck's strength is largely carried by its cards, so a competent but not expert pilot can still convert many draws.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Union Arena Standard midrange decks like this one involve a steady stream of Main Phase deployment and attack choices but relatively few branching sequences, and with a mono-colour base and heavy Edward duplication the line is fairly obvious most turns. Sequencing and response timing matter little since cards are used in one's own Main Phase, so timing sensitivity is low. The deck's weak, slow-start profile means misplays cost tempo more than the game outright, while the redundant Edward bodies let a competent-but-simple pilot win many games without fine play.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Sukuna Raid midrange involves a fair number of Main Phase decisions around energy-line development, Raid setup, and when to commit high-BP targets, but the core plan is fairly linear. Timing matters mainly in sequencing the Raid chain and holding interaction, while misplays in early development are costly against fast Aggro-Tempo decks, which makes errors significant but not razor-thin. Four copies of each core card and strong high-BP bodies mean the deck wins a good share of games on its cards alone.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Compared with other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this Purple Aggro shell is comparatively straightforward: deploy characters into the energy line, attack, and use Raid and Gatotsu when a window opens, with few per-turn branches. Its difficulty comes mainly from knowing when to commit into faster Aggro-Tempo and midrange matchups, and from managing Raid setup against a thin card pool, so errors are moderately punished but the plan itself carries much of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard the deck is a mid-tier tempo list where most turns come down to building the energy line, choosing which characters to play and which to attack with, and a few sequencing and race decisions per game. Its weaknesses against fast starts and the reliance on a developed energy line raise the cost of a clunky draw or misplay, while cheap bodies and the Test Type-01 payoff mean the obvious plays still win a fair share of games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Green Kirito is a straightforward aggro-tempo deck whose turns mostly reduce to deploying cheap Kirito and Sinon characters on curve and attacking, so most turns have one obvious line and the cards carry much of the win rate. Its skill demand comes from deciding when to commit to the board, when to attack into blockers, and how to race against faster Sakamoto Days or Evangelion decks, where errors in tempo are costly given its thin triggers and lack of recovery. Compared with the other competitive Standard decks, it sits in the lower-middle band for difficulty.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Red Asta is a dense, cheap aggro list whose turns are mostly obvious curve plays: deploy characters to the energy line and attack, with the AP budget as the main constraint. Its sequencing is simple and its errors are mostly recoverable, but it gives little help after falling behind, so the close games are decided by the pilot's attack and block choices, and its matchup spread is wide against faster Aggro-Tempo decks.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Red Inuyasha is a straightforward midrange shell: a mono-red energy line with playsets of Inuyasha and Kagome means the obvious curve-out wins many games, so decisions per turn and sequencing traps are modest. Its main skill demands come from choosing between front-line and energy-line plays and from reading matchups against faster aggro decks, which keeps matchup variance and error punishment moderate within the Standard field.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena tournament decks, this yellow Karane Inda swarm makes a modest number of meaningful decisions per turn, mostly deciding which characters to play into the energy line and when to attack with wide boards, which keeps decision density below midrange decks. Sequencing matters little because the bodies go down as drawn, and the deck has little reactive interaction to time, so timing sensitivity is low. It plays a fairly similar aggressive plan across matchups with small adjustments, and misplays like a few unnecessary attacks are usually absorbed by the cheap, redundant bodies. The cheap, consistent curve and reliable early board mean a new pilot keeps much of its win rate by simply playing out bodies and attacking wide, so autopilot factor is high.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Makima midrange-control deck asks for several real decisions most turns, including AP and placement across the front line and energy line, and its many Makima versions make the draw hand-dependent. Sequencing matters at key moments, but the timing demands are moderate rather than the tight response-window play of the most demanding decks. Its slow curve against fast attackers means misplays are often costly, while raw card quality offers some forgiveness; a new pilot would still lose much of the win rate without expert choices.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this midrange deck asks for several real decisions per turn: which Younger Toguro version to raid onto, when to build the energy line, and how to spread AP across the front line and energy line. Its sequencing matters around Raid timing and When Played triggers, but the core line is fairly legible. Errors are moderately punished, since a slow start against aggro can be fatal, while the deck's cards do a fair share of the work without a skilled pilot.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Kikoru Yellow Aggro is a straightforward curve-out deck: the opening sequence of Reno Ichikawa and Iharu Furuhashi is largely fixed, and most turns present one or two obvious plays, so decision density sits in the middle-low range for a competitive Union Arena deck. Sequencing matters mainly around when to commit the Kikoru threat and when to use Falling Thunder, while matchup variance is moderate because the deck's role shifts against faster versus grindier opponents. Error punishment is moderate since its weak trigger support and lack of finishers mean a misjudged race can lose, but the deck's raw pressure absorbs many small misplays; the strong autopilot factor reflects that the cards do much of the work when drawn well.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: As a Tier 2 aggro-tempo stack built around same-name Taro Sakamoto threats and cheap energy-line enablers, this deck makes straightforward turn-by-turn plays and rarely needs intricate sequencing, so it is relatively easy to pilot against other Standard decks. Its main skill demands are matchup-aware choices on when to commit threats and managing the thin spread of six Taro numbers, while the cards do much of the work when drawn cleanly.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Standard Union Arena, this midrange Purple deck makes several meaningful choices each turn about when to play large Sesshomaru versions, which energy line to build, and how to sequence Raid and When Played value from Naraku and Kagura, so it sits mid-high on decision density and timing. Its six split Sesshomaru versions and thin draw support make misplays and bad hands costly, while its strong bodies and Bakusaiga let it win on power once the board is set, keeping the autopilot factor moderate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Compared with other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this midrange-control Purple shell asks for several meaningful choices per turn around energy-line development, AP spending across turns, and which Natsuki Seba to deploy and when to move to the front line, which pushes decision density and timing demands into the middle band. Its cards are fairly self-driving for a steady early curve, but the slow ramp, lack of a finisher, and thin answers mean misplays and wrong matchup plans are noticeable rather than fatal, keeping error punishment and matchup variance moderate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, this midrange Osaragi list asks for a moderate number of decisions per turn, mostly around AP allocation on the awkward 1-2-3 ramp and when to commit characters to raids or BP battles. Sequencing and timing matter less than in trigger-heavy decks, since the list has little disruption and few response windows to manage. The deck's power is largely carried by consistent Osaragi and Taro draws, so a competent new pilot keeps much of the win rate, though its weakness to fast Aggro-Tempo decks means matchup knowledge still matters.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Red Arima midrange is a fairly straightforward Union Arena deck: its AP-ramp lines and key characters make turns mostly obvious, with a few real choices about when to commit characters and when to hold energy. Sequencing and timing matter modestly, and matchup adjustments are present but not drastic given the deck's narrow spread. Mistakes are moderately costly because the deck lacks removal and draw engines, but the strong midrange bodies and Kisho Arima finisher let a new pilot keep much of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Compared with other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Green Milim Aggro plays out fairly straightforwardly: the main job is to build the energy line quickly with cheap Ramiris and apply early pressure, so most turns hold one or two clear options. Its matchup spread is moderate, with the plan shifting mainly on whether the opponent stalls with large blockers or races on tempo, and a clunky opening hand is the main way a pilot loses outright. The deck's power comes largely from its cards, so a new pilot keeps much of the win rate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this midrange Ichigo Raid deck makes several meaningful choices each turn about energy-line development, AP allocation between Raid and Bankai, and when to attack, but the core plan of building the energy line and then Raiding with Ichigo is fairly direct. Sequencing matters mainly around AP limits and the Player One slow start rather than response windows, and misplays are usually recoverable thanks to the redundant four-copy core. The deck's power and stable draws let a pilot win a lot on card quality alone, though matchups against fast aggro decks require adjusting the plan.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Annie Leonhart Marley Green Midrange is a mid-tier, midrange deck whose decisions center on raid timing, AP spending between board development and attacks, and when to commit burst turns like Sneak Attack, so it asks for regular choices rather than constant branching. Its weak defense, lack of removal and slow finishing mean misplays against fast Standard decks are punished moderately, while its redundant raid lines and strong bodies let a new pilot win many games on the obvious plays.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Rukia Freeze Midrange asks for steady decisions each turn: when to commit energy-line bodies, when to build toward Raid steps, and which blocks or freezes to use. Sequencing matters around Raid timing and holding resources, but errors are usually recoverable given the deck's flexible board. Its draw is partly carried by a high count of Rukia copies and Bankai, so a competent but unrefined pilot still wins a fair share of games.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Standard Union Arena competitive decks, this Renji Raid-Midrange deck demands regular decisions about AP spending, energy-line sequencing, and when to Raid, with a high skill ceiling per the factor scores. Its Raid chain and the risk of stalled energy lines or lost upgrades punish sloppy sequencing moderately, while the four-copy Renji core gives it a fairly straightforward default game plan.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Bazz-B midrange has a dense low-cost base and a clear curve, so most turns offer a readable play, but the AP budget forces real development-versus-draw choices and the split Bazz-B variants add identification decisions. Its skill ceiling sits at the mid-range of the Standard field: the cards carry much of the win rate through the obvious curve, while matchup adjustments against fast aggro and the timing of the energy line reward a skilled pilot.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: As a Tier 2 midrange Yellow deck, Hisoka-led lists present several real choices each turn: which Gon or Killua to play into the energy line, when to spend AP on Raid upgrades, and what to hold back for the opposing board. Its four-of core and many interchangeable low-cost bodies keep most turns fairly obvious, so the cards carry a lot of the win rate, while Raid AP sequencing and the thin disruption suite mean misplays on the 1- and 2-AP turns can cost the game.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Green Kaiju No. 8 midrange deck asks for regular decisions about when to build the energy line, which Kafka Hibino numbers to deploy, and when to commit to Raid attacks, placing it above simple aggro shells but not at the top of the tier. Sequencing matters for setting up Raid and AP ramp on turns 1-3, yet most turns are fairly direct, and misplays are usually recoverable rather than immediately fatal. The thick Raid payoff line and plentiful bodies let a straightforward pilot win many games, though the close matchups against tempo decks and the spread of Kafka numbers reward experienced play.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Midrange Ten Swords builds with a cheap, consistent early board and a heavy finisher, so most turns have a clear default line with several real choices around AP spending and when to commit Shishio. Sequencing matters mainly in the tight first three turns (development versus optional draw), and errors are punished most against fast aggro decks, though the deck's power and predictable opening keep it forgiving for a competent pilot.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Union Arena Standard decks spread from simple aggro to intricate combo-style lists, and this midrange-tempo Air Cavalry shell sits in the middle: it demands Raid timing and a Lancelot-plus-target hand, but a straightforward curve of Suzaku bodies into Raid plays out fairly obviously. Its thin disruption and lack of card draw mean misplays in resource sequencing are noticeable, yet the cards carry much of the win rate on their own, which keeps the difficulty moderate relative to other competitive decks.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Standard Union Arena, this midrange Choi Jong-in Raid deck makes several real decisions per turn, weighing energy-line development against when to Raid and how to spread Raid targets and BP across the board. Its sequencing matters mostly around building the energy line before the 3-AP Raid turns, and a lost battle or removal costs two cards, so misplays compound. The plan is fairly stable against different opponents, but its slow start and lack of disruption mean the pilot must adjust how much to invest against aggressive decks.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Asuna Purple Midrange is a mid-tier deck whose turns mostly follow a clear curve of low-cost characters onto the energy line, with a few real choices about positioning between the energy line and front line and when to commit Kirito. Its plan changes modestly against aggro versus control, and misplays cost tempo rather than the game outright, but the lack of a finisher and thin trigger support make it demanding to pilot well relative to other competitive Standard decks.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Red Kaneki/Ayato Raid midrange asks for regular decisions about when to set up the Raid pairing, which bodies to commit to the energy line, and how to spend AP each turn, but the core line of playing cheap Kaneki and Naki into Raid is fairly readable. Its skill ceiling comes mainly from correctly matching the split card-number versions in hand and judging when Raid is worth the tempo, while the strong Half-Kakuja boost and Aogiri energy support let a straightforward pilot win many games.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Red Eren Raid midrange involves several meaningful choices per turn about which Eren version to deploy, when to commit AP and energy toward a Raid turn, and when to use Hardened Punch, which puts it above the simplest Union Arena decks. Sequencing matters around the energy line and Raid timing but is less punishing than control-style sequencing. Its power ceiling and four-copy consistency let a reasonable draw win on its own, so the autopilot score is moderately high, while the awkward mix of Eren versions and tight early AP makes misplays cost real tempo.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Union Arena Standard decks are generally straightforward to pilot, so this Raid midrange deck sits in the middle of the field: it asks for regular decisions about base selection, energy-line positioning, and when to commit to the Raid payoff, with real but not extreme turn-by-turn branching. Its slow turns 1-3 and reliance on a suitable base plus energy make errors costly against faster Standard decks, while the strong Aoi Todo and Mechamaru density means a reasonable draw still wins without precise play, keeping the autopilot factor moderate.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Kagurabachi Purple Iori Samura is a low-curve aggro-tempo deck built on full playsets of Iori Samura, so most turns have one obvious play and the deck is comparatively forgiving to pilot. Its main skill demands are attack timing with raid chains, deciding when to commit to the board against faster or stronger boards, and reading the matchup, which is where its moderate matchup spread and 44 skill ceiling come from.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Against the other competitive Standard decks, this mono-red midrange list makes several meaningful choices per turn: when to commit characters to the energy line, which base Chihiro to Raid onto, and whether to attack or hold blockers. Its timing demands are moderate, since most sequencing is in its own Main Phase with a few Raid and switch-to-active windows to track. Matchup variance is notable because it is a slow deck that must change plan against aggro-tempo opponents, while the Chihiro Raid chains give it a strong default that keeps autopilot play viable.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Red Boros Raid-Sonic is a mid-complexity tempo deck: the pilot must choose between deploying Sonic bodies, funding Boros by sending Sonics to the energy line, and when to commit Wind Blade Leg or Tempest Wind for battle, which adds real per-turn decisions beyond a straightforward curve. Errors are punished because the deck is linear with little draw or search, so a misjudged energy-versus-attack tradeoff or a Boros brick is hard to recover from, though the smooth Sonic opening keeps the simplest lines reasonably effective.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Rimuru Midrange in Union Arena Standard involves real positioning and Raid timing decisions each turn, with several viable lines whose consequences carry over, placing it above the simpler decks of the format. Its sequencing and energy-line management matter at key moments, but it is less punishing than the tightest tournament decks. Its Rimuru base and smoothing cards let a reasonable pilot win without perfect play, so the autopilot score sits near the middle.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Red Miroku is a straightforward midrange deck whose four-copy playsets of Miroku and Sango make the opening predictable, so the obvious line wins a good share of games, which keeps the autopilot score high. Its decisions are mostly about when to commit characters and when to fire Wind Tunnel or Hiraikotsu against the faster Heisuke, Rem and Bomb Devil decks, so decision density and matchup variance sit modestly above the simplest Standard decks. Errors are punished moderately, since losing the early tempo race to fast decks can be hard to recover from but there is little complex sequencing to get wrong.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Union Arena Standard tournament decks, this mono-green midrange deck makes a moderate number of meaningful decisions per turn, mainly around which characters to play to reach the green energy line and when to commit AP to attacks. Sequencing matters somewhat in getting the energy line online on time, but it is not a deep timing deck. Matchup variance is moderate because the deck has few answers and lacks tech options, so its plan changes less than a flexible deck would, while errors are forgiving only partially given its vulnerability to fast tempo openings. Its dense, consistent Mereoleona core lets a new pilot keep much of the win rate on autopilot.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena Standard, this Zeke midrange deck makes a moderate number of real decisions per turn, mainly around when to commit Pure Titans to the energy line and which Zeke copy to deploy, but the curve is fairly linear and the line is straightforward. Timing matters less than in trigger-heavy decks because the deck relies on sorting its own Main Phase plays rather than responding on the opponent's turn. Matchup variance is moderate since fast aggro decks force a different defensive posture but the game plan stays largely the same, and the lack of draw or disruption means misplays are costly when life is under pressure. Because Zeke copies and cheap Titans carry much of the win rate, the deck is fairly forgiving for a new pilot.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Envy is a midrange deck whose turns mostly revolve around the cheap Envy energy line, then choosing when to commit expensive Fathers and Bradleys and how to attack into the board, so it asks for a steady stream of moderate decisions rather than long branching turns. Timing matters at a few moments (holding Envy's responses and sequencing AP and energy) but not constantly, and the deck's listed weaknesses show that matchup adjustment against fast or trigger-heavy opponents is significant without being a per-game rewrite. Mistakes like a mulligan into too many expensive cards or a late Double Attack race are punished, but the playset consistency and solid bodies let a competent but imperfect pilot win a fair share of games, so the cards do a good part of the work.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Relative to other Standard Union Arena tournament decks, this midrange-tempo Crusch Karsten shell asks for a handful of real decisions per turn: sequencing the AP and energy line, choosing when to Raid onto a Crusch Karsten, and timing the event suite for tempo. Its high copy counts and simple early curve make the opening lines fairly obvious, so the pilot's skill matters most in mid-game sequencing and in mulligan decisions. Errors are moderately punished because the deck is slower than the faster Blue decks and has little recovery, but its strong BP bodies and repeatable interaction keep most mistakes recoverable.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Emilia is a midrange-tempo deck with a steady energy line and a wide Emilia package, so most turns involve a few real choices about front-line positioning, energy-line development and Raid targets, but many turns are still fairly obvious. Timing matters mainly in Main Phase sequencing and the Attack Phase, not in response windows, and misplays such as a stalled energy line or a slow Raid start are usually recoverable against midrange opponents, though fast aggro decks punish them hard. Its consistency and straightforward plays let a new pilot keep much of the deck's win rate, while matchup adjustments are moderate rather than a full change of plan.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Compared with other Standard tournament decks, this midrange Han Song-yi/Jinwoo raid shell asks for real per-turn choices about which energy-line body to raid into and where to place Cha Hae-in and Esil, but the core line is fairly direct. Raid sequencing and the early-turn gap against fast pressure decks add some punishment for misplays, while the strong Jinwoo payoffs keep much of the win rate on the cards rather than the pilot.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Sung Jinwoo Shadow Army Raid asks for many meaningful choices each turn: which cheap Shadow Soldiers to develop on the energy line, when to spend AP on a Raid upgrade versus fresh bodies, and which sideline recovery lines to pursue. Its skill ceiling is high and the high power ceiling and redundancy soften losses, but misjudging the early board or over-committing to the energy line against wide or fast Aggro-Tempo boards is punished, and the deck gives a new pilot less to lean on than the raw stats suggest.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Against other competitive Union Arena decks, this midrange-tempo Benimaru Ogre build plays out fairly straightforwardly: deploy cheap bodies on the AP curve, build the energy line, and attack for Raid or the main threat. Its redundancy and playsets of cheap characters make the obvious line win a good share of games, so it sits below the more demanding combo and disruption decks. Sequencing and misplays matter moderately, mainly around timing the Raid line and using Hell Flare, but a single misstep is usually recoverable.

skillRating.label: Advanced
skillRating.reasoning: Among competitive Union Arena Standard decks, the Purple Kaneki Raid-line asks for frequent decisions each turn: which Kaneki body to Raid, when to move to the front line, and how to split limited AP between deploying and attacking. Its Raid sequencing and the risk of losing a whole stack to one battle make single misplays costly, but the deck has a clear core and little reliance on responses, so it sits in the mid-upper range rather than the top. Matchup planning matters against fast aggro decks, though its overall game plan stays broadly consistent across opponents.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Rei Ayanami Yellow is a midrange-tempo deck where each turn involves several real choices: Raid target, line placement, and AP split, which gives skilled pilots an edge over the obvious play. Sequencing matters around the Raid chain but is not a constant precision demand, and misplays are usually recoverable thanks to solid mid-game bodies, though the Aggro-Tempo matchups punish slow setups. The deck's power is moderate and its draws are clunky, so a new pilot will not keep most of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Red Zenitsu is a low-curve aggro-tempo deck whose turns are mostly obvious deploy-and-attack lines, but it still asks real questions about when to commit the 4-copy burst events, which characters to hold back, and how to sequence AP and energy-line placement. Its matchup spread is wide, since the plan must shift between racing fast aggro and facing large midrange boards without removal, and misjudging the race or overextending into a sweep is punished. Its 4-of core makes autopilot strong, though the thin draw and lack of comeback tools mean a pilot still decides close games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Blue Levi is a midrange deck whose turns involve several real choices about line placement, AP spending, and which of the many Levi versions to deploy, but the Survey Corps cohesion keeps most cards on one plan. Sequencing and Raid timing matter at key moments rather than every turn, and the pilot's matchup reads against aggressive Re:ZERO and Sakamoto Days lists shift the plan meaningfully. Errors are moderately punishing because the slow start can be lost to pressure and a poor opening hand is hard to fix, while the deck's cards carry a fair share of its win rate.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Within Union Arena's Standard field, this midrange Raid deck asks for regular decisions about which characters to play into the energy line, when to Raid into the big bodies, and how to sequence Raid bases against the pressure of aggro decks. Raid timing and the near-duplicate naming of Annie, Pieck and Reiner cards add sequencing care, and a misplayed Raid chain or a lost top card leaves a real tempo hole. Much of its power still comes from the cards themselves, since the obvious curve-out and Raid plays win a good share of games without expert reads.

skillRating.label: Intermediate
skillRating.reasoning: Compared with other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, Purple Naraku asks for regular decisions each turn: when to deploy the Raid base versus hold it, how to pace the 1/2/3 AP ramp, and when to commit the Naraku payoff. Its Raid sequencing and Naraku's Raid condition mean a misordered turn or a stalled draw costs real tempo, and it is punished by faster aggro-tempo decks, but its key cards are straightforward once a base is on board, so the obvious line wins a fair share of games.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Modernia is a midrange deck whose core lines are fairly stable, so most turns have a clear default play and the redundant Marian/Rapi curve lets a pilot coast on obvious sequencing. Its main difficulty comes from judging when to commit Modernia versus holding resources and handling close BP battles, with matchup-specific pressure from fast Aggro-Tempo decks; within Standard's competitive field it sits in the middle band, with a fairly forgiving autopilot-driven baseline.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Green Saitama is a midrange deck with a smooth curve of cheap bodies, so most turns offer a clear line and only a few real decisions per game, notably when to commit Saitama and how to spend AP. Sequencing matters less than in control-style decks, and the deck's power and simple curve let a newer pilot keep much of its win rate, though close games and slow 1-2 AP starts still reward careful resource management.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Purple Yuna is a fairly straightforward midrange plan: build the energy line with Yuna and Kirito/Silica, then pressure with Asuna, so most turns have a clear default play. Difficulty comes from managing AP and sideline/removal-area resources, spreading across five Yuna variants, and deciding when to attack into high-BP defenders, with the list's lack of draw and answers making misplays harder to recover from. Relative to other competitive Union Arena Standard decks, its tempo and disruption are modest, so the autopilot factor is above average.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Yellow Asuna is a midrange Goddess trio whose plan is fairly linear: set the energy line, then deploy a Goddess once the required energy is present, so most turns offer few real choices. Sequencing matters mainly in the Main Phase when establishing the energy line and managing AP, and mulligan or AP-stall mistakes are costly given the thin early curve. Matchup variance is modest because the same board-filling plan is used across opponents, and a strong draw with duplicated key characters largely plays itself, which keeps the skill ceiling below the most demanding Standard decks.

skillRating.label: Beginner-Friendly
skillRating.reasoning: Within Standard Union Arena, this tempo deck is built around cheap Mari and Rei bodies that ramp the energy line quickly and play out smoothly, with repeatable four-of playsets making most turns fairly obvious. Its decisions center on AP allocation and when to commit against blockers, and its low disruption and absence of a finisher limit how often the pilot faces hard sequencing or timing traps, though close games still turn on AP efficiency and closing the game.

cardMetrics.name: Versatility
cardMetrics.desc: How many different decks or IP archetypes the card fits into, distinguishing cross-IP staples from IP-specific role-players.

cardMetrics.name: Power Impact
cardMetrics.desc: How much the card improves win rate when drawn or played, measuring its direct contribution to winning game states.

cardMetrics.name: Consistency Impact
cardMetrics.desc: How much the card contributes to reliable execution of the deck's core game plan through search, draw, or filtering.

cardMetrics.name: Meta Relevance
cardMetrics.desc: Current competitive usage rate and frequency across top tournament placements and winning decklists.

cardMetrics.name: Replaceability
cardMetrics.desc: How easily the card can be substituted without meaningful loss in deck quality; lower replaceability indicates higher importance.

cardMetrics.name: Synergy Value
cardMetrics.desc: How well the card enables or benefits from interactions with other cards in its archetype, measuring combo potential and IP-internal cohesion.
